note.question: How can non-ownership business models support solar energy?
note.overview: Solar power companies have introduced innovative non-ownership business models—leasing and power purchase agreement (PPA)—in addition to sales. Under these models, the company installs solar panels for a customer, who purchases the electricity generated from the panels. Under leasing, a customer pays a fixed fee, whereas under PPA, a customer pays a per-unit price for the electricity generated.

components.formal: Objective relation: Intuitively, customers with lower generation rely on the utility firm for all their electricity demand under a restriction on PPA, which limits solar panel adoption, resulting in lower generation.
conditions: Restricting the solar power company from offering PPA leads to lower total adoption and generation of renewable energy (N∗ SL ≤N∗and G∗ SL ≤G∗), resulting in a higher profit for the utility firm (π∗ U,SL ≥π∗ U).

Restricting the solar power company from offering leasing leads to higher total adoption and generation of renewable energy (N∗ SP ≥N∗and G∗ SP ≥G∗), resulting in a lower profit for the utility firm (π∗ U,SP ≤π∗ U) if and only if c < C3(α,β,r).

To understand the intuition behind the above result, consider the setting where in the absence of restrictions, the company prefers to offer leasing but not PPA (when c > C2(·) and α < A2(·); see Proposition 1).
